explanations.explanation: Canaanite is right. Judah, one of Jacob's sons, sees the daughter of a Canaanite man named Shua and takes her as his wife. Friend, he leaves his brothers, looks around, and he's married. That man did not wait for the boxes to get unpacked.

Egypt is where Joseph ended up after he was sold (Genesis 37:28). It's not where Judah finds his wife. The text says Shua is a Canaanite man. Judah is living near Hirah, an Adullamite, when he sees Shua's daughter.

I see where that came from. Midianite traders were the ones who passed by when Joseph was sold (Genesis 37:28). But Judah's wife isn't from them. The text says she's the daughter of a Canaanite man named Shua.

Wicked is the word. The text says Er, Judah's firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the LORD, so the LORD put him to death. It doesn't say what Er did, so I won't guess. I think this one is heavy, friend, and it's okay to feel that.

Proud is not the word the text uses. It says Er was wicked in the sight of the LORD. It doesn't tell us what he did, so I'm not going to fill that in. This part of the story is heavy, and the text keeps it short.

Foolish isn't what the text says about Er. It says he was wicked in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD put him to death. The writer doesn't give the details, so we leave them alone. It's a heavy moment, friend.

Right on target. Judah tells Onan, his second son, to perform his duty as her brother-in-law and raise up offspring for his brother. So the offspring would be Er's. Onan was handed a job for somebody else's name, and it's right there in Genesis 38:8.

That's the very thing Onan was unhappy about. Verse 9 says he knew the offspring would not belong to him. Judah's instruction was to raise up offspring for his brother. So the offspring would be Er's, not Onan's.

Her father doesn't come into this instruction at all. Judah tells Onan to sleep with his brother's wife and raise up offspring for his brother. The offspring is for Er, the brother who had died. Tamar's father only shows up later, when she goes to live in his house.
True. What Onan did was wicked in the sight of the LORD, so He put Onan to death as well. That's two brothers now. I'll just say it plainly, friend: this part is heavy.

It's True, though I understand hoping for something gentler. Genesis 38:10 says what Onan did was wicked in the sight of the LORD, so He put Onan to death as well. The text says it straight, with no extra details. This is a heavy part of the story.

explanations.answer: Live as a widow in her father's house
explanations.explanation: That's it. Judah says, “Live as a widow in your father's house until my son Shelah grows up.” (Genesis 38:11) So Tamar packs up and goes. Judah's youngest was the one she was waiting on.

explanations.answer: Stay and serve in Judah's own house
explanations.explanation: Judah sends her away, not into service. He tells Tamar to live as a widow in her father's house until Shelah grows up. The text says she went to live in her father's house. Nothing about serving in Judah's home.

explanations.answer: Go home and marry someone else
explanations.explanation: Judah doesn't say anything about her marrying someone else. He says, “Live as a widow in your father's house until my son Shelah grows up.” (Genesis 38:11) She goes home still a widow, waiting on Shelah. I'd have been tapping my mustache the whole time.

That's the opposite of what the text says. Judah's thought is, “He may die too, like his brothers.” (Genesis 38:11) So he doesn't feel Shelah is safe at all. Sending Tamar away is how he keeps his youngest at a distance.
False is right. Judah thinks, “He may die too, like his brothers.” (Genesis 38:11) That's the reason he gives for sending Tamar away to wait. A father holding his last son close, and I get that.
Shear is the word. Somebody tells Tamar that Judah is going up to Timnah to shear his sheep. Verse 12 says he's going to his sheepshearers there. Tamar gets the news, and she's listening.
Selling isn't the errand. The text says Judah is going up to Timnah to shear his sheep. It's his sheepshearers he's headed to (Genesis 38:12). Shearing is the job.

Watering is a fine shepherd job, but it's not this trip. Tamar is told her father-in-law is going up to Timnah to shear his sheep. That's the errand the text gives. Shearing day is the news she hears.
Not quite. Verse 14 says Tamar saw that although Shelah had grown up, she had not been given to him as a wife. Shelah is grown, but Judah hasn't kept his word. That's what Tamar sees.
False is right. Shelah has grown up, but Tamar had not been given to him as a wife (Genesis 38:14). Judah told her to wait until Shelah grew. The waiting is over, and nothing has happened.
A veil is what she uses. Tamar removes her widow's garments and covers her face with a veil to disguise herself. Then she sits where Judah will pass. A plan is in motion, friend.
A hood is a good guess, but the text names something else. Tamar covers her face with a veil to disguise herself. Verse 14 says she did it after taking off her widow's garments. Veil is the word.
She does hide her face, but the text calls it a veil. Genesis 38:14 says she covered her face with a veil to disguise herself. No mask in this story. A veil it is.
That's what the text says. When Judah saw her, he thought she was a prostitute because she had covered her face. He didn't realize who she was. Tamar's disguise worked, and it's all in verse 15.

The text doesn't say that. Judah sees a woman with her face covered, and he thinks she's a prostitute. That's the reason given in verse 15: she had covered her face. A shepherd's daughter doesn't appear in this scene.

Timnah is where Judah is headed, but he doesn't take her for a servant. The text says he thought she was a prostitute because she had covered her face (Genesis 38:15). He has no idea she's his daughter-in-law.
A young goat. Judah says, “I will send you a young goat from my flock.” (Genesis 38:17) He's promising to pay later. A promise alone is hard to hold, friend.
Close, since we're in sheep country. But Judah promises a young goat from his flock. The text says so in verse 17. It's a goat, not a lamb.
A ram would be a big promise. But Judah says, “I will send you a young goat from my flock.” (Genesis 38:17) That's what he offers to send. A young goat, and he'll send it later.

explanations.answer: His seal and cord and staff
explanations.explanation: That's the list. Tamar answers, “Your seal and your cord, and the staff in your hand.” (Genesis 38:18) Judah hands them over, and she becomes pregnant by him. Remember those three items, because they matter later.

explanations.answer: His ring and robe and sandals
explanations.explanation: Those are not the items she names. Tamar says, “Your seal and your cord, and the staff in your hand.” (Genesis 38:18) Judah gives her those. A seal, a cord and a staff.

explanations.answer: His cloak and belt and purse
explanations.explanation: That's a fair list, but it's not hers. Tamar asks for “Your seal and your cord, and the staff in your hand.” (Genesis 38:18) Judah gives her exactly those. Seal, cord and staff.
True. Judah sends Hirah with the young goat, and Hirah could not find her. Verse 20 says he went to collect the items Judah had left with the woman. He's got the goat, and she's gone.
Hirah doesn't find her. Genesis 38:20 says that when he went to collect the items, he could not find her. He's carrying a young goat and has nobody to give it to. A long walk, friend.

explanations.answer: No shrine prostitute has been here
explanations.explanation: That's their answer. The men of that place say, “No shrine prostitute has been here.” (Genesis 38:21) Hirah goes back with the same report. Nobody there has seen her.

explanations.answer: She left for Timnah that morning
explanations.explanation: The men don't point him anywhere. They answer, “No shrine prostitute has been here.” (Genesis 38:21) Nothing about her leaving for Timnah. Hirah gets no direction at all.
Hirah is an Adullamite, so I see why that one tempts. But the men give no direction. They say, “No shrine prostitute has been here.” (Genesis 38:21) That's the whole answer.

explanations.answer: So they won't become a laughingstock
explanations.explanation: That's his reason. Judah says, “Let her keep the items. Otherwise we will become a laughingstock.” (Genesis 38:23) He lets his seal, cord and staff go rather than keep asking around. Nothing else is given as the reason.

explanations.answer: So she won't come asking for more
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't give that reason. Judah says, “Let her keep the items. Otherwise we will become a laughingstock.” (Genesis 38:23) His worry is about being laughed at. Nothing about her coming back for more.

explanations.answer: So Tamar won't hear about it
explanations.explanation: Judah doesn't mention Tamar here, because he doesn't know it was her. His reason is, “Otherwise we will become a laughingstock.” (Genesis 38:23) He thinks he's dealing with a woman on the road. Tamar is not in his mind.

explanations.answer: That she be burned to death
explanations.explanation: That's what Judah says. He answers, “Bring her out! Let her be burned to death!” (Genesis 38:24) I think this one hurts to read, friend. Hold on, because the story isn't done with this moment.
The text says something harder. Judah answers, “Bring her out! Let her be burned to death!” (Genesis 38:24) He doesn't just send her away. It's a heavy moment, and the story turns right after it.
That's what Judah had not done, and Tamar knew it. His order is, “Bring her out! Let her be burned to death!” (Genesis 38:24) Marrying Shelah isn't on his mind here. It's a heavy order, friend.

explanations.answer: She's pregnant by the owner of these items
explanations.explanation: That's the message. Tamar sends word, “I am pregnant by the man to whom these items belong.” (Genesis 38:25) She doesn't name him. She lets the items do the talking.

explanations.answer: She's pregnant by Judah's son Shelah
explanations.explanation: She doesn't name Shelah at all. Her message is, “I am pregnant by the man to whom these items belong.” (Genesis 38:25) The items are the whole point. She doesn't give a name.

explanations.answer: She's pregnant by a man from Enaim
explanations.explanation: Enaim is where she sat by the road, but the message doesn't name a place. Tamar says, “I am pregnant by the man to whom these items belong.” (Genesis 38:25) Her proof is the items she holds.

Righteous is it. Judah says, “She is more righteous than I, since I did not give her to my son Shelah.” (Genesis 38:26) That's a hard thing to say out loud, and he says it. Friend, owning a mistake takes real nerve.
Reckless isn't what Judah says. His words are, “She is more righteous than I, since I did not give her to my son Shelah.” (Genesis 38:26) He's the one looking at his own part. Righteous is the word.
Judah turns it the other way. He says, “She is more righteous than I, since I did not give her to my son Shelah.” (Genesis 38:26) He's pointing at himself, not at her. Righteous is the word he picks.
True. When the time comes for Tamar to give birth, there were twins in her womb. Two babies, and the story has a surprise coming. Hang on, because the delivery gets busy.
It's True, so you've got a surprise coming. Genesis 38:27 says that when the time came, there were twins in her womb. Two babies, and the next verses are busy ones. Stay with me.
Wrist is right. The midwife takes a scarlet thread and ties it around his wrist. Then she announces which one came out first. A little bright thread on a very small arm.
An ankle would be a long reach in that moment. The text says one baby put out his hand, so the midwife tied the scarlet thread around his wrist (Genesis 38:28). The hand is what came out first.
A finger is a small target. The text says the midwife took a scarlet thread and tied it around his wrist (Genesis 38:28). The hand came out, so the wrist got the thread.

That's the surprise. The baby with the thread pulled his hand back, and his brother came out first (Genesis 38:29). So the midwife's announcement didn't hold. Thread on the wrist, and he's still second.

False is right. He pulled his hand back and his brother came out first (Genesis 38:29). The thread was tied on one baby, and the other one was born ahead of him. Nobody saw that coming, least of all me.
Perez it is. The midwife says, “You have broken out first!” and the text says, “So he was named Perez.” (Genesis 38:29) His brother, with the scarlet thread, is Zerah. The name matches what happened.
Hezron is a name from later in the family. Genesis 46:12 lists Hezron and Hamul as sons of Perez. So it isn't the baby's name here. The twin who broke out first is named Perez.
Hamul turns up later in the family. Genesis 46:12 lists Hezron and Hamul as the sons of Perez. So Hamul isn't the baby in this scene. The twin who broke out first is Perez.
